shortQuestions: Back e.m.f. ε_b = NBAω sin ωt (average ∝ NBAω): it depends on the number of turns, the magnetic field, the area of the armature coil and the speed of rotation.
It is always less than the applied voltage V, since I = (V − ε_b)/R must be positive for the motor to run; so it is limited by the supply voltage and the load (speed).
When the load (rate of doing work) increases, the motor needs more torque and slows down.
Back e.m.f. is proportional to the speed (ω), so it decreases.
The current I = (V − ε_b)/R then increases, giving the larger torque and power needed.
Induced e.m.f. ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt is proportional to the number of turns N.
Coils with many turns give a larger e.m.f. and current for the same flux change, so the galvanometer deflection is larger and easier to observe.
Unit of flux: 1 Wb = 1 T m² = 1 (N A⁻¹ m⁻¹) m² = 1 N m A⁻¹ = 1 J A⁻¹.
So ΔΦ/Δt has unit J A⁻¹ s⁻¹ = J C⁻¹ = V, the unit of e.m.f.
Dimensions: [Φ] = [ML²T⁻²A⁻¹], so [Φ/t] = [ML²T⁻³A⁻¹] = [ε]. The equation is dimensionally correct (the minus sign is dimensionless).
Flux linkage = NΦ = NBA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the coil.
For a coil rotating with angular velocity ω, θ = ωt: NΦ = NBA cos ωt, which is maximum (NBA) when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to B and zero when it is parallel.
A metal disc or plate attached to the moving wheel or rail passes between the poles of a strong electromagnet.
The changing flux induces eddy currents in the metal; by Lenz's law their magnetic field opposes the motion, producing a braking force.
Kinetic energy is changed into heat. The braking is smooth, frictionless and stronger at higher speed (used in trains and roller coasters).
Make the core of thin laminated sheets of soft (silicon) iron insulated from one another by varnish or oxide.
Lamination breaks the large eddy-current loops and the high-resistivity material reduces the current, so the I²R loss is small. (Ferrite cores are used at high frequency.)
Under the glass-ceramic top is a coil carrying high-frequency alternating current.
Its changing magnetic field induces eddy currents in the iron/steel base of the cooking pot.
The I²R heating of the eddy currents heats the pot directly, while the cooktop surface itself stays relatively cool.
When the armature of a motor rotates in the magnetic field, an e.m.f. is induced in it (generator action).
By Lenz's law this e.m.f. opposes the applied voltage and is called back e.m.f. ε_b. The armature current is I = (V − ε_b)/R; it is small at full speed and large at start-up.
In a radial field the plane of the coil is always parallel to the field lines.

The torque NIAB (and the induced e.m.f.) is then maximum and constant at all positions, giving smooth uniform rotation and a deflection proportional to current, instead of the varying torque NIAB cos α of a uniform field.
(a) Laminated soft iron.

(b) Soft iron has high permeability (concentrates flux, good flux linkage) and low hysteresis loss (easily magnetised and demagnetised). Lamination reduces eddy-current loss. Solid iron would have large eddy currents, and aluminium is non-magnetic.
longQuestions: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an e.m.f. (and current) in a circuit when the magnetic flux linked with it changes.

Experiment 1: a coil is connected to a galvanometer. Pushing a bar magnet into the coil deflects the galvanometer; withdrawing it gives the opposite deflection; no deflection when the magnet is at rest.
Experiment 2: a straight wire connected to a galvanometer is moved across the field between magnet poles — deflection occurs while it moves.
Experiment 3: two coils side by side; switching the current in the primary on or off induces a current in the secondary.

Magnitude depends on the rate of change of flux: speed of motion, strength of the magnet, number of turns and area of the coil (ε = −NΔΦ/Δt). Direction depends on the direction of motion/flux change and is given by Lenz's law (or Fleming's right-hand rule).
Faraday's law: the e.m.f. induced in a circuit is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with it: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt.

Statically induced e.m.f.: the conductor is stationary and the flux changes, e.g. switching or varying the current in a primary coil induces e.m.f. in a nearby secondary coil (mutual induction, transformer) or in the coil itself (self-induction).
Dynamically induced e.m.f.: the conductor moves and cuts magnetic field lines, e.g. a rod moved across a magnetic field (ε = BLv) or a coil rotated in a field (generator).
In both cases a galvanometer shows a deflection only while the flux is changing.
Lenz's law: the direction of the induced current is always such that it opposes the cause (change of flux) producing it.

Example: when the north pole of a magnet is pushed towards a coil, the near face of the coil becomes a north pole and repels the magnet; when the magnet is withdrawn, the face becomes a south pole and attracts it.
Hence work must always be done against this opposing force to move the magnet. This mechanical work is converted into the electrical energy of the induced current (and then into heat).

If the induced current aided the motion, the magnet would accelerate by itself and electrical energy would be produced without work — violating conservation of energy. So Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of energy.
Mutual induction: when the current in one coil (primary) changes, the changing flux linking a neighbouring coil (secondary) induces an e.m.f. in the secondary.
The flux linkage of the secondary is proportional to the primary current: N_sΦ_s ∝ I_p, so N_sΦ_s = MI_p.
Induced e.m.f.: ε_s = −N_s ΔΦ_s/Δt = −M ΔI_p/Δt.

Coefficient of mutual induction M: the e.m.f. induced in the secondary when the current in the primary changes at the rate of 1 A s⁻¹ (or flux linkage per unit primary current). It depends on the number of turns, areas, separation, orientation and the core material.
Unit: henry (H); 1 H = 1 V s A⁻¹ = 1 Wb A⁻¹.
Self-induction: when the current in a coil changes, the changing flux of its own field induces an e.m.f. in the same coil, opposing the change (Lenz).
Flux linkage is proportional to current: NΦ = LI.
Induced e.m.f.: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt = −L ΔI/Δt.
Coefficient of self-induction L: the e.m.f. induced in a coil when the current through it changes at 1 A s⁻¹. For a solenoid L = μ₀N²A/l; it increases with turns, area and an iron core.
Unit: henry (H), 1 H = 1 V s A⁻¹. Self-inductance opposes changes of current (electrical inertia), e.g. a choke.
Motional e.m.f. is the e.m.f. induced in a conductor moving through a magnetic field.
A rod of length l slides with velocity v on two rails perpendicular to a uniform field B. Each free charge q in the rod feels a force F = qvB along the rod, so charges separate and an e.m.f. appears.
In time Δt the rod moves vΔt, so the area of the circuit changes by ΔA = lvΔt and the flux changes by ΔΦ = BΔA = Blv Δt.
Faraday's law: ε = ΔΦ/Δt = Blv. (Equivalently, work per unit charge = Fl/q = Blv.)
If the rod moves at angle θ to B, ε = Blv sin θ; its direction is given by Fleming's right-hand rule.
A generator changes mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. A d.c. generator uses a split-ring commutator so the output current always flows in one direction.
A rectangular coil of N turns and area A rotates with angular velocity ω in a uniform field B. At time t the normal makes angle θ = ωt with B, so the flux linkage is NBA cos ωt.
Induced e.m.f.: ε = −d(NΦ)/dt = NBAω sin ωt = ε₀ sin ωt, with peak value ε₀ = NBAω.

ε is zero when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to B and maximum when it is parallel; it reverses every half rotation — an alternating e.m.f. Slip rings give a.c.; a commutator reverses the connections every half turn to give pulsating d.c.
An a.c. motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy using alternating current.

Construction: a rectangular coil (armature) on an axle between the poles of a magnet (or field winding), connected to the a.c. supply through slip rings and carbon brushes (a synchronous motor) — or, in an induction motor, a stator producing a rotating magnetic field and a cage rotor.

Working: the current in the armature in the magnetic field experiences forces F = ILB on opposite sides, forming a couple that rotates it. In the induction motor the rotating field induces currents in the rotor, and by Lenz's law the rotor follows the rotating field.
Uses: fans, pumps, washing machines and other household and industrial machines.
A transformer changes an alternating voltage from one value to another without change of frequency.
Principle: mutual induction. An alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing flux in a common laminated soft-iron core, which induces an e.m.f. in the secondary coil.
Since the same flux links every turn: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. For an ideal transformer (no losses) V_pI_p = V_sI_s, so I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s. N_s > N_p: step-up; N_s < N_p: step-down.

A laminated core (thin insulated sheets) is used because the changing flux induces eddy currents in the core; lamination breaks up their paths and greatly reduces the heating (energy loss). Soft iron also reduces hysteresis loss.
When the armature coil of a motor rotates in the magnetic field, it cuts the field lines and an e.m.f. is induced in it, as in a generator.
By Lenz's law this e.m.f. opposes the applied voltage V and is called the back e.m.f. ε_b. The net voltage driving the armature current is V − ε_b, so I = (V − ε_b)/R.
At starting the speed and ε_b are zero, so a large current flows; a starting resistance is used to protect the coil.

As speed rises ε_b increases and the current falls. Under a heavy load the motor slows, ε_b falls, and more current flows to give the extra torque. The back e.m.f. therefore regulates the motor's current and power: Vᴵ = ε_bI + I²R.
